items.t: GSK stock faces Zantac settlement as patent wins shape focus
sum: GSK plc faces a mixed legal and strategic backdrop as investors weigh a reported Zantac settlement against favorable developments in vaccine patent litigation. A roundup by MarketFrame on Friday, November 13, said coverage in the previous 24 hours centered on patent wins, the settlement, restructuring and valuation.

MarketFrame reported that GSK faces a Zantac settlement covering 2.2 billion US dollars. The agreement adds a significant financial charge, but the roundup also noted that it would address a long-running legal overhang linked to claims involving the drug. The settlement remains an important consideration for investors assessing litigation risk alongside the company's operating performance.

The most favorable development in the roundup was a broad European injunction in GSK's vaccine patent dispute with Pfizer and BioNTech. MarketFrame described the decision as a wide-reaching outcome in GSK's favor, while also noting that coverage differed in its assessment of the court result. For shareholders, the ruling keeps attention on the value of GSK's vaccine portfolio and the company's ability to defend its intellectual property.

GSK was also covered after resolving a vaccine patent dispute with Moderna. The arrangement was presented as supportive for GSK's patent position and access to vaccine technology, although the available report did not provide financial terms for the settlement. These legal developments sit alongside the company's focus on specialty medicines and its late-stage pipeline.

Another reported development was a global restructuring plan valued at 2.5 billion US dollars. MarketFrame characterized the program as a large cost-cutting effort while noting questions about execution momentum. The plan may shape how investors judge future efficiency gains, but the report did not provide a detailed implementation timetable or savings schedule.

GSK stock traded at 22.89 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:44 CET on Friday, November 13, 2026. The quote places the share in focus as investors balance legal liabilities, patent protection and the company's plans to improve operating performance.
The broader FTSE 100 market provides the relevant backdrop for UK-listed pharmaceutical shares as investors assess company-specific legal and pipeline news.

sum: The S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.3 per cent to 9153.20 after recovering from early losses, with BHP and technology stocks lifting the market. The advance came as Australian home-loan values recorded their largest quarterly drop since the series began in 2002.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 closed 0.3 per cent higher at 9153.20 on Wednesday as BHP and technology shares helped erase early losses. The Australian sharemarket advanced despite falls on Wall Street and a sharp decline in new home-loan values.

Investors returned to BHP during the session, pushing the mining company from a 1.8 per cent loss to a 0.9 per cent gain. The materials sector also recovered, after weighing on the market earlier in the day.
The index added 24.20 points. It followed a 1.1 per cent gain on Tuesday. The Australian dollar rose 0.2 per cent to US68.77¢.

The value of new Australian home loans fell 15.5 per cent in the three months through September, Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed. It was the biggest quarterly decline since the series began in 2002, and nearly twice economists’ forecast.

The figures point to weaker borrowing demand amid the Reserve Bank’s interest rate increases to control inflation. The market’s gains came as investors weighed that housing data against a mixed session among major shares.

Commonwealth Bank fell 1.2 per cent, surrendering early gains. The bank said its first-quarter profit rose 8 per cent to $2.8 billion, as business lending growth offset difficulty in mortgages during the housing slump.

Vodafone Group shares closed at 116.95 pence on the London Stock Exchange on Monday, November 9, 2026, up 0.39% from the previous close of 116.50. The move was small. Yet it is the kind of bounce that technical analysts watch closely in a downtrend: the shares rose toward their 20-day average without reaching it, and that pattern is the one bearish signal in the day's screen, with no bullish counterpart.

The trend is down. The stock trades below both its 20-day average of 118.64 and its 50-day average of 122.78, and the 20-day line sits under the 50-day line. A moving average is simply the mean closing price over a set number of sessions, so shares below both lines are being priced lower than their recent history. The 20-day average itself fell 0.88% over five days. There was no new crossover between the two averages on the latest session. The bearish alignment is already established rather than freshly formed.

Over longer windows the price has barely moved: a 0.09% gain over five days and a 0.21% change over one month. A stock that has gone nowhere in a month while sitting under falling averages is stuck rather than recovering. The 3-month range runs from a high of 132.07 to a low of 114.30, and the latest close sits at roughly 8% of the 20-day range. That puts it near the bottom of recent trading, just above the 20-day support at 116.50.

As shown in the chart, price is pressed against the lower half of the Bollinger Bands, the envelope drawn two standard deviations around the 20-day average. The bands sit at 121.70 (upper), 118.64 (middle) and 115.58 (lower), and the close registers a %B reading of 22%. In plain terms, the price is in the lower quarter of its normal statistical range.

Momentum indicators do not confirm the downtrend with conviction. The 14-day Relative Strength Index, which measures the pace of recent gains against losses on a 0–100 scale, stands at 43.6. That is neutral, below the midpoint but well clear of the 30 level that usually marks oversold conditions.

Three super growth stocks, Eli Lilly, Micron Technology and Nvidia, are being flagged as candidates for investors to consider if the market corrects, according to a Motley Fool analyst writing in early November 2026. The commentary followed a day on which the S&P 500 fell by more than 4%.

Eli Lilly (NYSE: LLY) makes the weight-loss drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound. Its shares have averaged annual gains of nearly 40% over five years and were up about 57% over the past year as of early November.
The stock looks somewhat overvalued, the analyst wrote. Its price-to-sales ratio recently stood at 14.7, against a five-year average of 13.3.

Third-quarter revenue rose 39% year over year, and management raised its full-year projections. Prices fell a little, but higher volume more than made up for it. Lilly is also expanding with an oral drug, Foundayo, and sells Kisunla for Alzheimer's disease, Ebglyss for eczema and the cancer drug Jaypirca.

Interested In GSK's (LON:GSK) Upcoming UK£0.17 Dividend? You Have Four Days Left
sum: Readers hoping to buy GSK plc (LON:GSK) for its dividend will need to make their move shortly, as the stock is about to trade ex-dividend. The ex-dividend date is two business days before a company's record date in most cases, which is the date on which the company determines which shareholders are entitled to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is an important date to be aware of as any purchase of the stock made on or after this date might mean a late settlement that doesn't show on the record date. This means that investors who purchase GSK's shares on or after the 12th of November will not receive the dividend, which will be paid on the 7th of January.

The company's next dividend payment will be UK£0.17 per share, on the back of last year when the company paid a total of UK£0.72 to shareholders. Last year's total dividend payments show that GSK has a trailing yield of 3.8% on the current share price of UK£18.90. Dividends are an important source of income to many shareholders, but the health of the business is crucial to maintaining those dividends. As a result, readers should always check whether GSK has been able to grow its dividends, or if the dividend might be cut.

If a company pays out more in dividends than it earned, then the dividend might become unsustainable - hardly an ideal situation. GSK is paying out an acceptable 73% of its profit, a common payout level among most companies. A useful secondary check can be to evaluate whether GSK generated enough free cash flow to afford its dividend. Thankfully its dividend payments took up just 41% of the free cash flow it generated, which is a comfortable payout ratio.
It's encouraging to see that the dividend is covered by both profit and cash flow. This generally suggests the dividend is sustainable, as long as earnings don't drop precipitously.

Companies with falling earnings are riskier for dividend shareholders. Investors love dividends, so if earnings fall and the dividend is reduced, expect a stock to be sold off heavily at the same time. So we're not too excited that GSK's earnings are down 2.4% a year over the past five years.
Another key way to measure a company's dividend prospects is by measuring its historical rate of dividend growth.

GSK shares tips for keeping mature brands fresh
sum: At a recent industry conference, Andrea Luker, vaccine marketing operations and compliance, congress and peer-to-peer lead at GSK, offered the audience a candid look into a persistent challenge in pharma marketing: how to keep speaker programs for mature brands fresh, credible, and compliant long after the initial excitement has faded.

Luker explained that mature brands face a unique set of pressures that newer products do not. “A mature brand doesn’t go away. There’s still a medical need for it. That’s why it’s still on the market. So it is up to us to continue to educate,” she said. Unlike a brand launch, where novelty carries momentum, mature products must justify their continued presence in speaker programs through evidence rather than enthusiasm.

That evidence doesn’t have to be just clinical. True differentiation, noted Luker, comes from context: new patient populations, emerging evidence, shifting practice barriers, misinformation or misunderstandings, and market disruptions that create a genuine, documentable educational gap.

This is where Luker’s “relevant, differentiated, and defensible” framework comes in, built around three foundational questions she said every team must ask before advancing a program. “Is it a unique educational question? Is there an educational need? And do we have documentation?”

Luker stressed that defensibility must be engineered from the very start of program design, not retrofitted after the fact. “Compliance starts at the design stage,” she said, pointing to elements like documented educational need, clear audience definitions, explicit learning objectives, and evidence mapping as the building blocks of a program that can withstand scrutiny.

The message is that there is always an educational need that is defensible and can be compliant in mature brand programs. Luker said, you just can’t rest on cosmetic updates. “It’s not just the surface ... It’s not that we just updated the title or our visuals, our brand colors have updated it. That’s not distinct,” she told attendees.

What's Behind GSK (LSE:GSK) Shares Slipping Despite Beating Quarterly Forecasts?
sum: - GSK's quarterly sales and core operating profit came in above market expectations, led by HIV and respiratory specialty medicines.
- Vaccine sales softened as Shingrix faced destocking in China and inventory effects in the United States, while meningitis products grew.
- Shares fell as investors focused on restructuring costs, currency drag and higher interest expense, leaving the FTSE 100 drugmaker near the lower end of its recent range.

GSK (LSE:GSK) Healthcare GSK plc (LSE:GSK) 1923.50 GBX +8.500 0.444% Last Updated at: 2026-10-27T16:36:00Z is trading near the bottom of its recent range this week after a quarterly update that, on the face of it, had plenty to like. Sales rose at constant exchange rates, gross margin widened on a better product mix and manufacturing efficiencies, and both revenue and adjusted earnings came in ahead of consensus forecasts. It is a notable update for market participants who follow Healthcare Stocks listed in London.

Yet the shares fell in early dealings on results day and have struggled to regain ground since. Market commentary has pointed to the detail beneath the headline numbers rather than the quarter itself, with investors fixing on charges linked to the Accelerate Growth restructuring plan, a bigger currency drag than previously expected and higher guided interest expense.

The standout performer was the specialty medicines division, which grew strongly and did most of the heavy lifting. Long-acting HIV therapies Cabenuva and Apretude posted rapid growth, while Nucala benefited from its launch in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Trelegy returned to growth in the United States, although management acknowledged continuing pricing pressure in the American inhaler market.

Research and development spending rose sharply as the company pushed a large number of late-stage studies through the clinic. GSK said it has begun a long list of pivotal trials this year and expects more to start before the year is out, underlining how much of the investment case now rests on pipeline delivery rather than legacy products.

sum: - The company’s newest approvals and label expansions should contribute meaningfully to revenue growth.

Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are dominating headlines and attracting much of investors' attention. There is a good reason for that. Some AI companies could produce life-changing returns if infrastructure spending continues to grow. However, there are also attractive investment opportunities elsewhere, particularly for income-seekers, including in the biotech industry. Let's consider one biotech stock long-term dividend investors should seriously consider buying in November: Gilead Sciences (NASDAQ: GILD).

Gilead Sciences has performed well this year. The company's shares are up 39%, while the S&P 500 has climbed a comparatively unimpressive 11%. The biotech leader owes its strong showing in 2026, at least so far, partly to excellent financial results. And the company's third-quarter update added even more fuel to that particular fire.

In the third quarter, Gilead Sciences' revenue increased by 7% year over year to $8.3 billion. Let's remember that Gilead Sciences is still dealing with declining sales of Veklury, a coronavirus medicine. Demand for COVID-19 products -- be it vaccines or therapies -- has decreased substantially in recent years. Gilead Sciences' product sales excluding Veklury grew 16% year over year.

The company continues to lean on its core therapeutic area, HIV, to do most of the heavy lifting. HIV product sales came in at $6.2 billion, up 18% year over year, largely driven by Biktarvy and Descovy for PrEP, the company's most famous HIV drugs. Gilead Sciences' liver disease portfolio also performed well, posting revenue of $927 million, up 13% year over year.

These two segments performed well enough to offset the 18% year-over-year decline in cell therapy sales and the 69% year-over-year decline in Veklury's revenue. On the bottom line, Gilead Sciences posted non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.55, up 3% compared to the year-ago period. Overall, it was a solid quarter for Gilead Sciences, sending the stock higher post-earnings.

sum: London's blue-chip index outperformed most global markets on Friday 30 October 2026, with pharmaceutical, telecoms and energy heavyweights cushioning a sharp fall in NatWest and a global technology selloff.

The FTSE 100 closed at 10,729.78 on Friday 30 October 2026, up 7.71 points or 0.07% from Thursday's close of 10,722.07. London's index opened higher and rose about 0.5% in the first hour of trade, according to InstaForex, before giving back most of that advance as the global technology selloff deepened and Wall Street opened sharply lower. The small gain was nonetheless enough to secure the FTSE 100's first monthly rise in three months.

The index's resilience stands out on a day when Japan's Nikkei 225 fell more than 2%, Nasdaq futures dropped more than 2% and Germany's DAX 40 retreated. The FTSE 100's heavy weighting toward pharmaceuticals, energy, consumer staples and mining, and its relatively light exposure to technology, has made it a natural refuge during the latest bout of AI-related selling.

AstraZeneca, one of the three largest companies in the index, was among the leading risers after reporting third-quarter revenue of $16,209 million, up 7% at constant exchange rates, and core earnings per share of $2.79, up 19% at constant exchange rates. The drugmaker reaffirmed its full-year guidance and announced a restructuring programme expected to save around $1.5 billion, which it said would support long-term ambitions including investment in new drug pipelines.

AstraZeneca shares closed about 7% higher, the stock's best day in a year according to Reuters reporting, and GSK added around 2.5%. The broader pharmaceutical sector gained 5.1% over October, its biggest monthly rise since February. Because AstraZeneca carries such a large index weighting, its rally alone more than offset the losses in banks and miners.

NatWest Group was the biggest drag on the index and the worst performer in the STOXX 600, closing nearly 9% lower after its third-quarter net interest income fell short of analyst expectations. The bank reported attributable profit of £1,532 million and operating pre-tax profit of £2.23 billion, up from £2.18 billion a year earlier, with total income of £4.64 billion.

items.t: GSK Shares Sink 7% As Weak Vaccine Demand Rattles Investors Despite Profit Beat
sum: A sharp sell-off in GSK (GSK.L) stock on Wednesday signalled deep investor unease, with shares dropping 7% in morning trading despite the drugs giant beating profit expectations.
The culprit was a disappointing vaccine division, where quarterly revenues slipped 2% to £2.6 billion in the three months ending September 30.

Two of the company’s flagship vaccines drove the decline, with shingles treatment Shingrix posting a 5% drop and RSV shot Arexvy suffering a steeper 24% fall amid weakening demand in the United States.
The retreat in vaccine revenues overshadowed what was otherwise a solid set of numbers for the British pharmaceutical group, which is listed on the FTSE 100.
Core operating profits, stripping out exceptional items and currency movements, climbed 5% to £3.08 billion, comfortably ahead of the £2.93 billion analysts had anticipated.
Pre-tax profits told a different story, however, falling to £1.94 billion in the quarter compared with £2.5 billion during the same period a year earlier.
Bright spots emerged elsewhere in the business, with speciality medicines revenues growing 15% and cancer treatments delivering a 23% jump, helping cushion the vaccine shortfall.

items.t: FTSE 100 Rises to 10,694.50 as Banks Rally on a Lower Than Feared Budget Surcharge While GSK and Housebuilders Slump
sum: London's blue-chip index recovered from early losses on Wednesday, 28 October 2026, closing 7.96 points higher after Chancellor John Healey's first Autumn Budget proved milder for lenders than markets had feared.

The FTSE 100 closed at 10,694.50 points on Wednesday, 28 October 2026, up 7.96 points or 0.07% from Tuesday's close of 10,686.54. The gain was small, but the shape of the session mattered. The index opened lower, traded as low as roughly 10,643 in the morning as GSK and Unilever sold off on results, and only recovered after Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Autumn Budget to Parliament at 12:30 p.m. London time.

The close followed a 0.75% fall on Tuesday, when HSBC and Reckitt Benckiser dragged the index lower on disappointing third-quarter numbers. The mid-cap FTSE 250, which is more exposed to the domestic economy, fell about 0.3%, reversing an earlier rise to a near two-month high.

The headline measure for the stock market was the bank surcharge. Healey raised the corporation tax surcharge on banking profits from 3% to 6% for a temporary 15-month period. Investors had feared a larger increase, with some speculation that the levy would return to its former 8% level, so the announcement triggered relief buying across the sector. RBC Capital Markets analyst Benjamin Toms estimated that the change would be a net headwind of up to 4% for bank profitability in fiscal 2027.

The Budget also included cost-of-living measures, among them scrapping standing charges on gas bills, and the Chancellor said fiscal headroom would narrow to around £15 billion in 2029-30. Market reaction was calm overall, with sterling little changed at about $1.3310 against the US dollar by the London close. Gambling stocks gained after duty changes came in gentler than expected, while housebuilders were hit by a lack of clarity on the timeline and funding of a new first-time buyer scheme.

Banks led the recovery. Lloyds Banking Group closed up 1.7%, Barclays rose 1.6% and NatWest gained 2.0%, according to PA Media, while Standard Chartered added 2.4% after raising its full-year income growth and return targets. StanChart's third-quarter pretax profit jumped 27% to $2.25 billion, beating estimates on strong wealth management and trading income. Gambling operator Entain rose 3.6%.

Why Is GSK (LSE:GSK) Stock in Focus Today Ahead of Its Wednesday Update?
sum: - Vaccines, specialty medicines and HIV remain the focal points.
- Tariff policy and pricing pressure in the United States are background themes.

GSK plc (LSE:GSK) Healthcare GSK plc (LSE:GSK) 1923.50 GBX +8.500 0.444% Last Updated at: 2026-10-27T16:36:00Z is among the blue chips scheduled to update investors on Wednesday, in a week that also brings several of its sector peers. Pharma is a heavyweight corner of London's market, so the tone coming from the company is likely to influence sentiment toward the wider healthcare group. The news keeps the company firmly on the radar of readers who follow UK Blue-Chip Stocks.

The business is organised around vaccines, specialty medicines and general medicines. Its HIV portfolio, particularly long-acting injectable treatments, has been a long-running engine, while shingles and respiratory vaccines supply a second pillar. Observers will want to see whether demand patterns in those areas are holding as expected.

Late-stage assets in respiratory disease, oncology and liver conditions are among the programmes followed most closely. Updates on regulatory filings, trial read-outs and any bolt-on dealmaking can change the narrative quickly, and the company has been active in business development as it prepares for the loss of exclusivity on older products.

United States drug pricing and trade policy loom over the whole industry. Management commentary on tariffs, manufacturing investment and the way American government programmes may shape reimbursement is likely to be parsed carefully, because the US is the single biggest market for most large drugmakers.

Large pharmaceutical groups must constantly replenish their medicine cabinets, and acquisitions and licensing agreements are the quickest way to do that. GSK has been willing to strike deals for early and mid-stage assets, so listeners will pay attention to any hint about where it wants to add strength next, whether in oncology, immunology or infectious disease.

FTSE 100 Climbs to 10,724.86, a Three-Week High, as AstraZeneca, GSK and Defence Stocks Lead
sum: London’s blue-chip index closed at its highest level in three weeks on Wednesday, powered by a late rally in pharmaceutical, defence, energy and consumer staples shares, even as hot US inflation data hit Wall Street.

The FTSE 100 closed at 10,724.86 on Wednesday, 14 October 2026, up 74.53 points or 0.70% from Tuesday’s close of 10,650.33. The index opened almost unchanged at 10,649.97, dipped to a session low of 10,641.22 in the first hour of trading and then climbed steadily, hitting an intraday high of 10,731.30 shortly before the close.

London outperformed most major markets on the day. Its heavy weighting towards healthcare, energy, defence and consumer staples, sectors investors tend to favour when inflation and interest rates rise, allowed the index to shrug off a 1.1% fall in the S&P 500 and a 1.9% drop in the Nasdaq Composite.

The official close was 10,724.86, a gain of 0.70% and the index’s highest finish in three weeks. The FTSE 100 now sits about 2.4% below its 52-week high of 10,989.45 and roughly 15.6% above its 52-week low of 9,276.91. Over the past year the index has risen close to 14%.

The intraday path was notable. After a quiet morning, the index briefly fell back towards 10,660 around 13:30 London time, when the US consumer price index was released, before buyers returned. The strongest leg of the rally came in the final hour, taking the index from about 10,690 to above 10,720 by the 16:35 closing auction.

Housebuilder Barratt Redrow was the top performer, rising 4.70%, followed by Burberry, up 3.71%, and AstraZeneca, which gained 3.40%. GSK climbed 3.59%, making pharmaceuticals the biggest contributor to the index’s rise given the two companies’ combined market value. Unilever added 2.5% and British American Tobacco gained 0.8%.

Defence stocks were also in demand as the conflict involving Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia escalated. Babcock International rose about 3.5%, BAE Systems added 2.2% and Rolls-Royce gained 1.2%. In energy, Shell rose 1.2% and BP added 0.7% as Brent crude held near $106 a barrel.

Marston's shares surge as pub firm bets on sports bars
sum: The pub firm said its new Grandstand format, which offers big screens and match-based food and drink offers, has been a standout performer this year
Shares in Marston's surged on Tuesday after the hospitality group announced plans to accelerate the conversion of more than 100 of its pubs into sports bars.
The West Midlands-based pub operator revealed that its new "Grandstand" format, featuring large screens and match-day food and drink promotions, has been its "standout" performer this year.

While the World Cup delivered a significant boost in revenues for Britain's pub operators over the summer, Marston's is banking on sports enthusiasts to sustain its sales well beyond the tournament. Shares in the company climbed nearly 20 per cent to 55p on Tuesday morning.
The group's programme to transform its existing pubs into new formats is "now a proven engine of growth, with Grandstand the standout performer," it told shareholders.
Marston's overhauled 60 of its pubs into new formats last year and plans to refurbish a further 100 next year, with the majority earmarked for the Grandstand concept, as reported by City AM.
These sports bar conversions deliver a 30 per cent uplift in sales on average, the group said, and a return on invested capital of more than 30 per cent.

GSK plc Stock (GSK) Moved Down by 5.22% on Apr 29: Drivers Behind the Movement
sum: GSK plc (GSK) moved down by 5.22%. The Pharmaceuticals & Medical Research sector is down by 0.80%. The company underperformed the industry. Top 3 stocks by turnover in the sector: Eli Lilly and Co (LLY) down 2.47%; AbbVie Inc (ABBV) up 3.27%; Kalvista Pharmaceuticals Inc (KALV) up 38.79%.

GSK's share price experienced a significant downward movement today, largely influenced by a complex reaction to its first-quarter 2026 earnings report. While the company delivered robust top-line growth, including increases in total sales and core operating profit, and reaffirmed its full-year guidance, the market's response was notably negative.

A primary factor contributing to the decline was an unexpected shortfall in reported earnings per share relative to analyst consensus estimates, which appeared to overshadow the otherwise strong operational performance and positive pipeline developments. Although sales and core profit exceeded some expectations, investor focus on the earnings per share figure triggered a cautious reaction.

Broader market sentiment also played a role. Some investors engaged in profit-taking after a recent upward trend in the stock, questioning whether current valuations were fully justified by the long-term outlook. Furthermore, general market weakness, driven by macroeconomic concerns and risk aversion, created an unfavorable environment for the stock. Persistent concerns surrounding legal provisions and the anticipated decline in sales from older, general medicines also weighed on investor confidence, despite strong performance from specialty medicines and vaccines like Shingrix.

Despite these pressures, GSK highlighted continued momentum in its R&D pipeline, with new product approvals and significant regulatory progress for key assets like bepirovirsen for chronic hepatitis B. The company also confirmed its full-year 2026 guidance, projecting continued growth in sales and core operating profit, suggesting management's confidence in its strategic direction despite today's market reaction.

GSK delivers strong Q1 performance and start to 2026
GSK (Q1 Results): strong start, no upgrade
sum: GSK’s first-quarter sales landed broadly as expected, rising 5% to £7.6bn excluding currency moves. Growth in speciality medicines and vaccines more than offset a decline in general medicines.
A favourable shift in product mix and cost reductions helped drive underlying operating profit up 10% to £2.7bn.
Free cash flow increased by £0.1bn to £0.8bn, and net debt stood at £15.6bn.
A quarterly dividend of 17p per share was declared with 70p expected for the year as a whole. The ongoing £2.0bn buyback program has £0.3bn left to run.
2026 guidance is unchanged, as is the 2031 sales outlook of over £40bn. This year’s sales are expected to grow by 3-5%.

GSK’s first quarter shows solid progress towards full-year targets. While the valuation has lost some of its froth in the weeks leading up to results, it still felt like investors wanted more on the day.

There are plenty of pipeline catalysts to watch out for this year, with key clinical read-outs weighted to the second half. Although compared to 2025, the focus has moved slightly away from product approvals towards late-stage trials, pushing the probability down and the timeline out for potential commercial success. GSK’s recent success rate has been impressive, but it’s important that this trend continues if it’s to offset the impact of forthcoming patent expirations.

items.t: Young & Co Brewery Announce Update on Move to the Main Market March 25, 2026
sum: Young’s, the premium operator of pubs and bedrooms in London and the South of England, today provides an update on the proposed admission of: (i) its entire issued A ordinary share capital (the “A Ordinary Shares“) to the equity shares (commercial companies) category (the “ESCC“) of the Official List of the FCA (the “Official List“); (ii) its entire issued non‑voting ordinary share capital (the “Non-Voting Ordinary Shares“, together with the A Ordinary Shares, the “Ordinary Shares“) to the non‑equity shares and non‑voting equity shares category of the Official List; and (iii) the Ordinary Shares to trading on the main market for listed securities of the London Stock Exchange (the “Main Market“) (together “Admission“).

Further to its announcement on 22 January 2026, the Company now expects that: (i) Admission will take place at 8.00 a.m. on 28 April 2026; and (ii) the Ordinary Shares will be cancelled from trading on AIM at 8.00 a.m. on 28 April 2026. The last day of trading in the Ordinary Shares on AIM is therefore expected to be 27 April 2026. Admission will be effected through an introduction of the Company’s existing Ordinary Shares and the Company is not offering any new Ordinary Shares nor any other securities in connection with the proposed Admission. Accordingly, the Company hereby gives notice of the intended cancellation of trading of its Ordinary Shares on AIM in accordance with Rule 41 of the AIM Rules for Companies. Such cancellation is not subject to shareholder approval.

Admission remains subject to a number of conditions, including: (i) the approval by the FCA of a prospectus and the A Ordinary Shares being admitted by the FCA to the ESCC category of the Official List and the Non‑Voting Ordinary Shares being admitted by the FCA to the non‑equity shares and non‑voting equity shares category of the Official List; and (ii) admission by the London Stock Exchange of the Ordinary Shares to trading on the Main Market.

Shareholders should note that the Ordinary Shares will no longer be traded on AIM with effect from Admission and should take their own financial and taxation advice regarding the consequences of Admission.
Peel Hunt and Stifel are acting as Joint Sponsors exclusively to the Company and no one else in connection with the proposed Admission.

items.t: Stockwatch: a FTSE 100 stock to play end of Iran war
sum: US President Donald Trump beside Air Force One this week. Photo: Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images.

Perhaps it shows how ingrained a “buy the drop” approach has become since 2008, if not 1987, that risk assets roared back after US President Donald Trump’s latest shouty upper-case post about how Iran and the US are productively discussing “TOTAL RESOLUTION OF OUR HOSTILITIES”.

It looks very much as if Trump has blinked first amid the economic cataclysm unfolding and awareness of how his threat last Saturday – to obliterate Iranian energy facilities – would mean escalated retaliations. Oil prices took off, which would destroy Republicans at mid-term elections.

Iran remains in a strong position. It retains control of the Strait of Hormuz as leverage over the US and its allies, forcing the US to recalibrate. Clearly, Trump’s prime objective is no longer regime change but to reopen the Strait. Did any of his advisers recall how the Suez Canal was shut for eight years following the 1967 Six-Day War?

Urgency was underlined just before this surprise turn of events by a chief of the International Energy Agency (IEA) declaring this crisis as “equivalent to the combined force of the twin oil shocks of the 1970s plus the fallout of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on the gas market”. It would compromise “vital arteries of the global economy”, including petrochemicals, fertilisers and helium – an essential aspect for microchips and artificial intelligence (AI) besides hospitals.
While Iran’s foreign ministry and state media denied any talks, this probably was a show of strength to Iranians. I speculate that intermediaries had dialogue somewhere along the line.

Wegovy and Ozempic maker forecasts sharp drop in revenue for 2026
sum: The maker of Wegovy and Ozempic, Novo Nordisk, has predicted a sharp drop in revenues this year owing to what its boss described as a “painful” push by Donald Trump to lower US weight-loss drug prices, rising competition, and the loss of important patent protections.

Denmark’s Novo, once the poster-child for the growth in weight-loss treatments, said sales this year were likely to fall between 5% and 13%, ending years of double-digit gains, despite the promising launch of its new Wegovy pill in the US.
Its share price plummeted 17% on Wednesday, erasing all gains so far this year. In the past year the stock has lost nearly 50% of its value.

Last year, Novo’s total sales grew by 10% to 309bn Danish kroner (£36.6bn) “despite being a challenging year for the company”, according to Mike Doustdar, the chief executive. Profit before tax rose by 3% to 130.5bn kroner.

Doustdar said: “Our 2026 guidance reflects a year of unprecedented pricing pressure,” adding he hoped the “painful” impact would be an “investment for our future”. He hoped to sell higher volumes of obesity and diabetes drugs over the coming years, saying: “We are seeing a volume response to lower prices.”

He pointed to Novo’s agreement with the Trump administration to cut prices heavily, from more than $1,000 a month (£730) to an average price of $350 (£255), and the patent expiry of semaglutide, the main ingredient of its obesity and diabetes drugs, in several countries including India. That would allow generic drugmakers to make cheaper versions of Novo’s drugs. It has also been hit by cheaper compounded versions of its jabs made up by pharmacies, used by many Americans.
Novo will, however, keep patent protection for semaglutide in Europe and Japan until 2033, and in the US until 2032.

GSK (FY Results): another step towards mid-term target
sum: GSK’s full-year sales grew by 7% before currency movements to reach £32.7bn. Speciality medicines were the key contributor, up 17%, as cancer treatment sales rose over 40% on strong patient demand and new use cases for certain medicines.
Underlying operating profit was up 11% to £9.8bn, slightly better than forecast and reflecting the positive impact of a shift to higher margin products, and efficiency gains.
Full-year free cash flow grew 41% to £4.0bn, helped by profit growth and lower investment in physical assets. Net debt was £14.5bn (2024: £13.1bn).
The 2026 growth guidance range is 3-5% for sales and 7-9% for underlying operating profit. The 2031 sales outlook of over £40 billion remains unchanged.
GSK declared a quarterly dividend of 18p per share, taking the full-year total to 66p.

Luke Miels’ first set of results in the GSK hotseat were reassuring. While guidance didn’t veer far from market forecasts, retention of his predecessors’ mid-term sales target helped provide a further boost to sentiment on results day.

There are plenty of pipeline catalysts to watch out for this year. Although compared to 2025, the focus has moved slightly away from product approvals towards late-stage trials, pushing the probability down and the timeline out for potential commercial success. GSK’s recent success rate has been impressive, but it’s important that this trend continues if it’s to offset the impact of forthcoming patent expirations.
